rationale: B wins because it knows where the bodies are buried: "Substack says its top creators earned $400M — the number it won't break down is the story" turns the missing denominator into the angle instead of wallpapering over it. A has sharper ambition, but "$400 million in creator earnings is an inconvenient number for the subscription fatigue narrative" imports a whole outside discourse the facts did not provide. The founder can pitch from B after tightening two overclaims; A needs sourcing surgery before it stops freelancing for reality.
gaps_in_A: "$400 million in creator earnings is an inconvenient number for the subscription fatigue narrative" drags in a broad subscription-fatigue thesis not supplied in the update. Maybe true, but unsupported context is still unsupported.
"YouTube runs on ads" and "TikTok monetize through algorithmic distribution and advertising" lean on outside competitor framing. Useful after sourcing; not cleanly grounded in the provided facts.
"implying $40M or more flowed to Substack from top creators alone" is fragile math from an undefined creator-earnings figure. If "earned" is gross vs. net, the inference changes.
"a specific writer with 10,000 paid subscribers" invents a toy protagonist. A customer angle needs a real creator or it stays a reporting hypothesis.
gaps_in_B: "without the ad model" overstates the supplied facts. The update says Substack takes a 10% subscription cut; it does not say video or the feed carry no ads or no other revenue.
"revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions" is too absolute for a private company unless Substack confirms there are no other revenue lines.
"Substack doesn't want to be a newsletter company anymore" assigns motive. Make the product shift carry the argument; don't pretend to read the company's diary.

The set is a little too quick to bury the creator-operator angle. Refusing "One writer's leap from newsletter to video star" is correct, but a grounded version with a real Substack creator would be useful.
